summary.text: The hadal zone is the deepest region of the ocean, lying in long, narrow, V-shaped trenches from about 6 to 11 km below sea level.
Its 46 habitats cover less than 0.25% of the world's seafloor, yet trenches make up over 40% of the ocean's depth range.
Life there faces total darkness, low temperatures, scarce nutrients and extremely high pressure, and most of its organisms are scavengers and detritivores.

items.prompt: Going from sea level down to 90 m, water pressure rises ten-fold. How much does it rise going from 6,000 m down to 11,000 m?

options.label: It rises a hundred-fold
It only doubles
It rises ten-fold again
It rises a thousand-fold

items.explain: Pressure rises ten-fold in the first 90 m, but only doubles between 6,000 and 11,000 m.

items.prompt: The word "hadal" was chosen for the ocean's deepest trenches as a nod to which figure?

options.label: Poseidon, Greek god of the sea
Hydra, the many-headed monster

items.prompt: No sunlight reaches the floor of a deep trench. Where does most of the food and carbon there come from?

options.label: Fallout from upper layers, drifting sediment and landslides
Seaweed growing along the steep trench walls
Phytoplankton blooming in the trench's open water
Heat from the rock turned directly into food

items.explain: The main sources of nutrients and carbon are material falling from upper layers, drifts of fine sediment, and landslides.

items.prompt: Fish seem unable to live on the very deepest trench floors, though some invertebrates do. What mainly keeps fish out?

options.label: The near-freezing temperature
The total lack of light
The extreme pressure
The lack of other fish to eat

items.explain: Because of the extreme pressure, fish with backbones may have a theoretical maximum depth of about 8,000 to 8,500 m.

items.prompt: In the dark of the hadal zone, which living things make food from scratch?

Giant amphipods grazing the mud
Snailfish feeding on marine snow

Darkness and extreme pressure make it hard

paragraphs.heading: The deepest part of the sea
paragraphs.text: The hadal zone is the deepest part of the ocean, found inside ocean trenches. It runs from roughly 6 to 11 km below sea level, in long, narrow dips in the seafloor shaped like a V. There are 46 separate hadal habitats, and together they cover under 0.25% of the seafloor. Even so, trenches make up more than 40% of the ocean's range of depths. Most of them are in the Pacific.

paragraphs.heading: Naming a new zone
paragraphs.text: For a long time the hadal zone was lumped in with the abyssal zone above it. Then in the early 1950s, two separate expeditions, the Danish Galathea II and the Soviet Vityaz, found that the kinds of animals change noticeably at 6,000 to 7,000 m. In 1956 Anton Frederik Bruun proposed the word hadal for waters below 6,000 m, after Hades, the ancient Greek god of the underworld. Because the change is gradual, some, including UNESCO, now set the boundary at 6,500 m instead.

paragraphs.heading: Life under extreme conditions
paragraphs.text: Trenches are among the least explored and harshest places in the sea: totally dark, cold, short of food and under enormous pressure. At the deepest known point, 10,935 m, pressure tops 1,100 standard atmospheres. Food and carbon arrive mostly as material falling from above, drifting fine sediment and landslides, and most residents are scavengers or feed on debris. By 2020 more than 400 species were known from these depths, many with special adaptations.

paragraphs.heading: Giants, dwarfs and fish limits
paragraphs.text: Many hadal species live nowhere else. Some groups grow unusually large, such as amphipods and isopods, while others, such as nematodes and copepods, are unusually small. Only a few kinds of fish are known here, including snailfish, cusk-eels and some grenadiers. Pressure may stop bony fish from living below about 8,000 to 8,500 m, but some animals without backbones, such as bigfin squid and certain sea cucumbers, have been found below 10,000 m.

paragraphs.heading: Life without sunlight
paragraphs.text: The only primary producers known from the hadal zone are certain bacteria. They feed on hydrogen and methane given off when rock reacts with seawater, or on hydrogen sulfide from cold seeps. Some of these bacteria live inside the mantle of certain bivalves. Apart from them, the food web starts with creatures that eat marine snow, both fine particles and the odd carcass.

paragraphs.heading: Going down to look
paragraphs.text: Darkness and pressure make the zone hard to explore, so instruments must survive a thousand atmospheres or more. Crewed and robotic submersibles, with cameras and arms for collecting samples, let scientists study it in detail. Not all survive: the robot Nereus is thought to have imploded at 9,990 m in the Kermadec Trench in 2014. The first people to reach Challenger Deep, the deepest known spot, in the Mariana Trench, were Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh in 1960.
